claims.text: Local chemical segregation in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles lowers the energetic barrier for melting.
Surface enrichment of lower-melting-point elements initiates premelting below the premelting temperature of a homogeneous solid solution.
High-temperature rapid mixing yields homogeneous, well-mixed Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu solid-solution nanoparticles.
Lower-temperature mixing followed by controlled annealing induces partial elemental segregation at nanoparticle surfaces and subsurfaces.
The intervention compares cohorts engineered to differ in chemical homogeneity while they undergo identical in-situ TEM and DSC thermal protocols.
The proposed mediator is the degree of surface and subsurface chemical segregation.
Cu is treated as a lower-melting-point constituent whose local enrichment is especially relevant to premelting.
Local enrichment of lower-melting constituents reduces the local free-energy barrier to melting.
The reduced local melting barrier produces early surface premelting in segregated nanoparticles.
Homogeneous nanoparticles do not develop comparable compositional gradients.
Homogeneous nanoparticles consequently have a sharper melting transition at a higher onset temperature.
Segregated nanoparticles will develop local liquid-like domains earlier than homogeneous control nanoparticles.
Segregated nanoparticles will exhibit broader DSC features across the premelting regime than homogeneous controls.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles between 30 and 50 nm when oxidation and environmental effects do not perturb mobility or surface chemistry.
Substantial particle-size changes or external conditions that alter diffusion kinetics may cause deviations from the proposed behavior.
Analogous findings in bimetallic systems support the proposed segregation-based mechanism.
The diffusion kinetics and coupling between surface reconstruction and chemical segregation in this high-entropy system remain unquantified.
Nanoparticle morphology and intrinsic strain may introduce additional variation in the measured thermal response.
